artboards.title: Today — one radio, and it is in the garage
A — the puck runs the errand
B — everything you already own is an ear
C — the glass already in the room does it
The failure — nothing in the house can hear it

annotations.text:
WHERE A HUB IS, AND WHERE A LIGHT IS

A hub goes where the Ethernet and the socket are: a garage, a cupboard, under the stairs. A strip goes where the household wants light. Our own door is Bluetooth, from the one radio inside the box, and Bluetooth will not cross that.

THIS IS MEASURED, NOT FEARED. On a Pi on 21 September: at -51 dBm an SRP6a session establishes first try; at -64 dBm the link dies three to five seconds in, every attempt; at -25 dBm it completes. Thirteen decibels is the whole difference, and a real strip is taped behind a television, which is a metal plane, in another room. Two software levers were tried and neither closed it -- what is left looks like RF. docs/strip.md item 15.

WHAT SHIPPED INSTEAD IS AN APOLOGY. The wall now says "set it up in the same room as the hub, then put it where you want it". It is honest, it is a real improvement on the four different sentences that preceded it, and it quietly repeals "put the hub wherever you like" -- which is a promise the box makes. It is also not always possible: a mini PC hub may have no Bluetooth radio at all.

THE SHAPE OF THE ANSWER IS ALREADY DECIDED, AND IT IS NOT UP FOR ARGUMENT HERE. Whatever hears the strip is a courier. The hub opens the SRP6a session and the strip closes it, so the courier carries bytes it cannot read, and the press gate stays on the strip where item 23 put it -- a proxy that cannot decrypt and cannot press a button adds no trust surface at all. What these three boards argue about is WHO the courier is.

A IS THE PUCK, the thing we already ship that already has a radio, already speaks MQTT to the hub, and is already in the hallway because that is where it has to be for the wall switches. B IS EVERYTHING, every powered thing of ours reporting what it heard, with the hub asking the loudest. C IS THE GLASS, the wall panel doing it over Web Bluetooth, which needs no hardware and makes the household meet a chooser full of the vocabulary this whole design has been deleting.

RECOMMENDATION: A now, built so that B is only a longer list later -- the hub asking "who can hear this" is the same question whether one thing answers or four. C stays drawn and unbuilt, as the record of why the wall is not the radio. And the failure board is not a rival: it is the screen all three end at, and it has to be one sentence.

AND, AS EVER, "SOMETHING ELSE -- I'LL DESCRIBE IT" IS A REAL OPTION. The intended answer has been outside the candidate set on this canvas before.

TODAY -- AND IT IS THE PROMISE, NOT A BUG

Drawn from what ships: the last branch of app/src/StripSheet.vue carrying the brain's own sentence from brain/hub/strip.py:460.

The floor plan and the -72 are illustrative; the three measurements underneath are real and are the only numbers on this canvas that are.

The log on the right is the evening this was learned. Four failures, four different true-sounding sentences, and every one of them sent somebody to check a thing that was not wrong. The hub had the signal strength the whole time and threw it away. It keeps it now and replaces whatever the radio said with the distance whenever the strip was under -60 dBm -- which is why the collection's failure board insists on one cause and one sentence.

A -- THE PUCK RUNS THE ERRAND

The hub hands a job to something that CAN hear the strip, over the MQTT session that already exists between them, and the puck does the GATT work: scan, connect, write what it was given, report what came back.

The sealed tube across the middle of the board is the whole security argument. One SRP6a session, opened at the hub and closed at the strip; the puck is the corridor. It can drop an errand. That is all it can do.

WHAT IT BUYS, and no other board buys this: the household does nothing differently and no screen ever says the word "puck". It also frees the hub's own radio entirely, which is what makes a NUC with no Bluetooth an ordinary hub rather than a broken one.

WHAT WAS UNPROVEN IS NOW MEASURED, AND THE BOARD ASKED IT THE WRONG WAY ROUND. The puck is ALREADY a GATT central -- the mesh proxy link IS a GATT connection to a switch. The real question was a SECOND concurrent central link, and on 23 September a puck held one to a knocking strip for 61 seconds while the mesh link stayed up, the broker stayed connected and a wall switch obeyed three on/off cycles. 42 exchanges, 16 KB out in 384-byte long writes over an MTU of 69, 5 KB back, no failures, nothing dropped. docs/strip.md item 38.

WHAT IT COSTS IS THE MESH'S RATE, NOT ITS LIFE. Idle, 291 proxy PDUs a minute; with an errand running, 64. The last-PDU age goes from under half a second to about one and a half. So an errand that never ends is a puck that is permanently slow, and THE PROTOCOL HAS TO HAVE AN END. And the scan is worse than the link: six seconds of active scanning stops the mesh dead, zero PDUs, so the hub should hand the puck AN ADDRESS rather than send it looking -- the strip has already been heard by something, and Add is the one moment when spending the radio is free.

AND THE SEALED TUBE IS NOW MEASURED. A whole adoption has gone through a puck -- SRP6a, the press, the Wi-Fi and the hub details, nine exchanges and 17.5 seconds -- with the hub's own client driving it and the puck carrying blobs it was never given a key for. The Wi-Fi was refused until somebody pressed the button on the strip. docs/strip.md item 39.\n\nTWO THINGS THE PROTOCOL HAS TO ANSWER, and neither redraws this board. NimBLE leaks about two and a half mbuf blocks per exchange and then fails a write with rc=6, which is out of memory and NOT a dropped link although it reads as one -- so the press wait, 120 seconds polled every 0.7 s, must not be a GATT round trip each time. And a knocking strip rotates its BLE address and is missed by one ten-second scan in three, so the errand has to carry a sighting that is still warm. STILL UNPROVEN: distance. Every link measured was -35 to -79 dBm, with item 15's cliff at -64, so what a strip behind a television does to a puck in the hall is not known.

AND THE HOLE IN IT: a house whose first purchase is the strip has no puck, and that is the house most likely to be setting something up. That case is board B's argument and the failure board's second screen.

B -- EVERYTHING YOU ALREADY OWN IS AN EAR

The same errand as A without the single courier. Every powered thing of ours reports the strength it heard a knock at; the hub ranks them and asks the loudest.

WHAT IT BUYS OVER A is that it stops treating the hub's radio as special -- it becomes one ear that happens to be in the wrong room -- and it gets better the longer somebody has owned our things, with no particular thing required. The ranked list is also a measurement, which is what lets a failure name a ROOM instead of a distance.

WHAT IT COSTS is that a GATT central and an errand loop go into the smallest thing we ship: into a plug, into a strip whose one job is to be a light and not to stutter while it runs somebody else's handshake. It is A's unproven risk taken four times over.

AND IT DOES NOT FIX THE FIRST PURCHASE. A house with one of our things in it still has no ear.

SO IT IS PROBABLY NOT A RIVAL. Build A's question as "who can hear this", answered by one thing today and by a list later, and B costs nothing extra to arrive at.

C -- THE GLASS ALREADY IN THE ROOM

Web Bluetooth, in the browser the panel is already running in. No hardware, no firmware, and the screen is usually in the room being lit.

THE BOARD IS DRAWN AROUND THE ONE THING THAT CANNOT BE DESIGNED AWAY: the browser will not hand a page a radio without putting its own chooser in front of it first. That chooser is the screen the whole of design/door/ exists to avoid -- two strips in a box are PROV_52e20 and PROV_2e425, the addresses rotate between scans so the row is different every time, and the household is asked to identify their own light by a string. The object was supposed to be the identity: it is the one that is lit.

THREE THINGS HAVE TO BE TRUE AND NONE HAS BEEN TRIED HERE. A secure context, and the wall is served plain http on the LAN. A browser with the API, and the wall is an Android WebView, not Chrome. And somebody standing at the glass, because the gesture is the permission model -- so this cannot run at three in the morning and cannot run from a phone in another house.

KEEP IT DRAWN AND UNBUILT, the way design/door/ShowMe.dc.html is kept: it is the record of why the wall is not the radio.

THE FAILURE, AND IT IS NOT A FOURTH DIRECTION

Every answer here fails the same way and all three end at this screen, so it is drawn once.

TWO SHAPES, AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME SCREEN. One is a thing that knocked too quietly to finish, which is a failure and is reported as one -- and the gain over the shipped sentence is that it can name the nearest ear, so the household is told WHICH ROOM rather than "the hub". The other is a house where nothing is listening at all, which is not a failure because nothing ever knocks: today it is a wall that stays empty while a strip advertises in the next room for forty-eight hours. That one is said in Add, before anything is tried.

THE RULE UNDERNEATH is the one this whole collection is downstream of. One cause and one sentence; below -60 dBm the distance IS the reason and whatever the radio said that minute is discarded; never two reasons, because that is the household checking both; and no dBm on the wall ever -- "the nearest thing that can hear it is in the hall" is a measurement in the only units a household has.
